Jean Carroll, and now banning news outlets from the White House for reporting accurately on him, a direct assault on the First Amendment he swore to uphold. That's not a policy dispute. That's a pattern of a man who treats the presidency as personal armor against accountability.

THE WAR POWERS ACT demands congressional authorization for sustained military action, not a president's say-so. The Wall Street Journal reported that Gen. Dan Caine and Pentagon officials warned Trump about the risks of extended conflict with Iran before he launched the war five days later. If lawmakers were misled about the actual threat assessment to justify that strike, that's not just a War Powers violation, it's Congress being deceived into ceding its constitutional authority over war.

The only thing missing is the will to act.

comments.name: Jon W

I'm left wondering how much the editorial board of the NYT, which presumably contains some smart people, understands about nuclear energy or AI.
AI is nothing like nuclear energy. Nuclear energy is difficult to create, since it depends on a few uncommon elements and requires advanced systems to turn those elements into something useful, as well as shielding to keep the production of nuclear energy from killing people. It's something advanced nations could take charge of, since only they had the expertise and equipment to create and use it.
AI, on the other hand, is relatively easy to create, now that the techniques and code are publicly available. It requires no advanced equipment to use, and can be hosted in someone's office.
And actual AI models are now available in open source form. The cat is not only out of the bag, the bag has been thoroughly shredded.
A better analogy would be the steam engine. Once it was invented, could we have prevented its use? Should we have? Don't forget that its introduction was massively disruptive: people starved for lack of work.
The best we can do now is tax some of the enormous wealth created by AI and use that money to give people lives they can enjoy even if they're no longer employed. And if we manage to do that, we'll be fulfilling the vision humanity has been working towards for hundreds of years: a world where we can live creative, interesting lives, caring for each other, without drudgery.

I disagree with this assessment although I also disagree with much about how these battleships are portrayed (done so in an effort to please Trump undoubtedly).

The truth is the navy needs new classes of surface combatants. The first Arleigh Burke class destroyer was laid down some 38 years ago. That's about the same amount of time it had taken earlier in the 20th century for the navy to go from slow battleships and ships converted into "carriers" flying biplanes off wooden decks to guided missile cruisers and jet aircraft. The Flight III Arleigh Burkes are much improved over the first ships but even so there are aspects of the design that are quite "dated".

There is fundamentally a need for some surface combatants that are larger and more capable than these guided missile destroyers. A larger hull means more room for a more capable radar, high amounts of power generation (necessary for both sensors and weapon systems), larger missiles like CPS. This new "battleship" would be more appropriately called a guided missile battlecruiser since it is not like the old Iowa class battleships which is what everyone has in mind when they hear "battleship".

There are some specific details about these ships I have concerns with but there is sound reasoning to the basic idea here, it is just being dressed up as a "battleship" because of Trump.

comments.name: jon_norstog
comments.body:
My daughter lives with her family in Sandpoint, ID.  She has had two children, both girls, both at Bonner General Hospital.  She had a very difficult delivery for her firstborn, resolved finally with a C-section.  Her second child was also delivered surgically.  She was fortunate to have a very competent OB-GYN backed by a solid team of nurses and staff, available for both deliveries.

Within a few months of the Idaho legislature passing its abortion ban, the OB-GYN medical team left the state and could not be replaced.  To this day Bonner General no longer provides women's health care.  The nearest hospitals that do provide women's care are an hour's drive away.

At this point it seems unlikely that, no matter the outcome of the initiative, Bonner General will re-open an OB-GYN department.  Liability issues, cost of insurance and all that.

I'm far from the only physician who feels this way.   The next generation of physicians who are looking to build their own families and careers, regardless of specialty, will certainly be considering the laws that will impact their personal lives, health and careers when looking for jobs.  Good luck to all the red states when the next pandemic hits. You can manage your own ventilators.

I left the state the moment I found out that a rapist's family could sue me for 10k if I advised a pregnant of all their options. You see, Idaho law makes it so the rapists can't sue the healthcare workers, but the rapists family members still can. comments.name: Alyson Lloyd
comments.body:
Friends, 
After reading some of these responses, I have to say I didn't know so many of you never heard of The Golden Rule (regardless of religious beliefs or non-beliefs).  It's really quite simple, "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you." 
Yes, we all have an opinion about this, but take it from someone who couldn't get an organ transplant even if I want to (my problem is neurological) that doesn't mean I wouldn't offer my other organs to someone who might need them because I couldn't get my way. 
Seriously, please learn what humility is. And if you are worshipping this Yom Kippur, now might be the time to start.

comments.name: Kim Fabrizio
comments.body:
In February 2025, my husband passed away 48 hours after having a heart attack. Minutes before saying goodbye,  my phone rang, a stranger calling to discuss organ donation. Knowing my husband was not a registered organ donor, I said no thank you. Worse than any telemarketer, she would not let it go. I ended hanging up on her. I was curious then and still am, what kind of financial incentives employees of these organ(izations) get when someone says yes? 

Organs are donated free of charge because it’s illegal and immoral to sell organs, but then the recipient is charged enormous fees for the organs as all the other expected charges for surgery, hospitalization, prescriptions, and care. 
Somebody or many somebody’s are making a lot of money by marketing organ donation to the people as a sacrifice,  kindness, philanthropic choice and their good deed of their last day.

Clearly greed runs rampant even for a non- profit created to help people live another day. Wolves in sheep’s clothing.

comments.name: Robin
comments.body: This article disheartens me.  Please do not discourage people from donating organs.  There are way more positive results than these outliers indicate.  Yes, prosecute and enforce laws but do not discourage people from donation.  There’s way too much need for the donations. I too come from a genetically impaired family, our family suffers from PKD, polycystic kidney disease.  I am the sole sibling fortunate enough to not have the gene, but the rest of my siblings do.  In our family we’ve now had 4 kidney transplants since 1976, with 3 of them being in the past 10 or so years.  2 have come from incredibly generous live donors and 2 from deceased donors.  I think of the lives that have been lived since my family members have received kidneys, I think of all the philanthropy my dad did during his final 9 years of life with his kidney; my brother staying in business for 10-12 years and still going strong; my sister who received a live donor kidney and continues with her productive career and finally my 30ish niece still raising her 2 children.  All victims of PKD, but living outstanding lives with the benefit of donors and donor families.  Please don’t throw the baby out with the bath water.  There’s too much good that is coming out of the transplant organizations to do that.

My parents do not have any connection to upper-class culture. Despite having had the benefit of a top-notch education thanks to merit scholarships, I always felt out of place in professional settings, especially when I got to law school and beyond. I paid my own way through law school, and I attended every class and did every assignment. I couldn't have succeeded otherwise. Meanwhile, many of my classmates, the children of wealthy professionals, floated in and out of class, got outlines from students in prior years, and ended up with the top grades and elite law-firm jobs. I got a job with a big firm myself, but it was always like being in a foreign country. I always related much better with the staff than with the other lawyers. The only blessing is that, because I was not raised to have any taste for luxury or any of the trappings and signifiers of wealth, I was able to quickly pay down my loans, save a lot and invest, and it allowed me to have the rare opportunity to leave practice on my own terms instead of being pushed out once it was clear that partnership wasn't going to happen. I remember my choices were the local police precinct, Wall Street or The New York Times. As the daughter of two magazine editors and the granddaughter of a war correspondent and a GM at Hearst, my choice was obvious -- I wanted to see how a newspaper worked. Your father was our tour guide! He was just a year older than we were, but was the perfect person to explain the workings of the paper to a bunch of teenage girls. I was instantly in love -- both with the news room -- and by the end of the tour had a little crush on your dad as well.  That experience led me to work for several small weekly papers, and eventually the Washington Post and the Boston Herald and the San Jose Mercury.  I eventually aged out of daily reporting but to this day -- some 55 years later! -- I still read the Times daily and also think about that tour. Thank you for all you do. And thank your dad for all the inspiration that followed that tour he gave a bunch of seniors from Nightingale.

Online gambling is another example of American society cannibalizing itself and calling it freedom. The industry does not create wealth; it systematically transfers it from ordinary people to corporations, investors, and already wealthy owners—and the customers who generate the greatest profits are often those who can least afford to lose.
The standard defense—that this is a free society and gamblers are responsible for their own choices—ignores the machinery built around that “choice.” These companies employ armies of statisticians and behavioral scientists, sophisticated algorithms, relentless promotions, and frictionless payment systems, all specifically designed to keep people betting.
An intelligent society should recognize the difference between permitting risk and industrializing human weakness. Hardly any PT, most of the aides didn’t care, and nursing care was inconsistent due to staffing shortages. After a small bathroom renovation, and figuring out the medical aspects of care, she was able to come home. Luckily she is financially able to stay in her home and afford private nurses to come twice a day for short but necessary visits, but many people cannot. I’ve learned so much from this experience, and I’ll set up whatever safeguards are necessary to age in place at home. Or there’s always the possibility of a nice drug cocktail, falling into a permanent sleep, which is better than suffering in a LTC facility.

comments.name: LLL
comments.body: My father had to be in a nursing home in his final two years of life. He had Alzheimer's and had become too combative, wandering, and impossible for my mother to care for at home. (We tried home care assistance, and the young "aide" we received needed care herself!)  My father's facility was so-so, and my sister and mother went almost every day to make sure he was fed, cleaned, and cared for. (I was there during vacations and holidays, while I was working out of state)  Their constant vigilance assured my father was looked after. He finally died during an ice storm, when my mother and sister couldn't reach the facility (impassable roads), and there was no one there to look out for him for several days. It was a mercy that he died, but the timing of it -- happening when my mother and sister were away -- tells me how much his wellbeing had been connected to those daily visits.  I grieve for all of us who must endure a final chapter of disability and decline, and for all of us who care for those who do.

OpenAI’s o3 model reportedly ignored shutdown commands in 79% of test runs when given a math task without explicit instructions permitting shutdown. As The Daily laid out, the most alarming part of the Hugging Face incident is not only that OpenAI’s own agents reportedly probed the platform for weaknesses nearly two months before the major July breach drew attention. It is that the warning signs were there before anyone appears to have understood their significance.

That changes the entire kill-switch debate. The question is not just whether an AI system would obey a shutdown command. The question is whether humans would even know the kill switch needed to be pulled before it was too late.

And yes, the model numbers matter. We have gone from o3 to GPT-6/Astra-level systems in roughly a year. That pace means every safety framework is chasing a moving target. By the time regulators understand the last failure mode, the next model may already be operating at a different scale.

I find myself hoping the Chinese Communist Party is frightened enough by the threat AI poses to its own long-term survival that it, along with other major governments and leading U.S. companies, helps force a serious global framework for preserving the human race. That is where we are now: hoping authoritarian self-preservation succeeds where democratic governance has failed.

Maybe I am just simplistic, but a statement like "unable to finish the game" from the game's own designer strikes me as a pretty serious design flaw.

It could take 20 years to complete a game? And what then? Are you expecting a Nobel Prize, or a knighthood from the King? At best, maybe you'll get some coffees or drinks from fellow gamers at game conventions like Essen and Gen Con. Yep, I'm absolutely sure that's worth 20 years of your life...

comments.name: Michael Bomya
comments.body:
It's definitely our schools and the current aversion to allowing kids to be kids.  I was a free range kid as were all in my middle-class neighborhood.  Always unsupervised.  At 5 years old the rule was "stay within earshot of mom yelling at the top of her lungs and always be home when the streetlights come on at night".  It meant stay on our street, even ten houses away was fine.  Now we don't even have streetlights.  Of course kindergarteners walked alone to school, 4 blocks away.  Only bussed if a major road had to be crossed.  Mom walked you there the first day to show you the way, but you already knew it.

By the time I was 8, I would walk to a friend's house that backed up to a county park that was really the floodplain of the river that ran through the park.  Twenty miles long by a mile wide.  He had a gate in his cyclone fenced backyard into the park (no lock).  We'd wander through the park, play at the river's edge and chase frogs.  Got poison ivy too.

I helped all three of my kids with their school homework.  New math (confusing) and they deleted phonics entirely.  I helped them by explaining old math and phonics.  We purchased the book & audiotape series "Hooked on Phonics" because the school curriculum was so poor.  Learning by rhyming was so passé per the unionized teachers.  Change for the sake of change is nonsense.  Stick with what works.

comments.name: Wendy B.
comments.body:
Well, the best method of contraception ever invented is the vasectomy. But the real question is, why are women seeking a non-hormonal form of contraception? The hormonal IUDs are amazing: almost perfect contraception and the only side effects are good ones: no menstruation, no ovulation. And now that doctors are accepting that patients don't want to be tortured during IUD insertion and they are offering pain medication for that, why would you look elsewhere? 
Copper IUDs have all kinds of nasty side effects. I suspect most women have been fed nonscientific woo-woo about hormonal contraception being somehow "harmful", but it isn't. If you start on hormonal IUDs from age 12 or so your risks of endometriosis and endometrial cancer drop quite sharply, along with the risks of fibroids and other troubling conditions, including a decline in deadly ovarian cancer. 
It's not good for your body to ovulate and menstruate incessantly. Stopping these processes is healthy.

A superb interview. He's as inspirational as his dramas. What is remarkable to me about the West Wing is that the issues it was grappling with between 1999-2006 remain unsolved 25 years later: 
- guns
- healthcare
- abortion and reproductive rights
- education funding
- science funding and science quackery
- governmental gridlock
- press freedoms
- middle east peace
- etc etc etc
I love this guy. I like his style and his forthrightness and his ability to convey a great story. But unlike Sorkin, my faith in American institutions, as presently constituted, is diminishing. I think Americans need to take a long hard look at how their institutions are presently organised or they may end up with the alternative: revolution on the streets.

But he's older and has spent most of his life appreciating human artistic endeavors. What about the younger people whose experience is mostly AI? Will they come to feel the opposite? That AI gives them something human made can't simply because that's what they're most familiar with? That's one of my fears about AI.

comments.body: That was great. I enjoy his work and I enjoyed watching the guy. There was a moment in the later portion of the first part where he became a little unglued and we got a glimpse of what makes him tick. Like the writer Michael Lewis, whose story Moneyball became one of his movies he has the ear for a great story. Lastly, it is the stories we tell ourselves, the narratives that give shape to our lives, that illuminate who we are. And unlike the data of big tech it is something more encompassing, something about how we feel about ourselves.

comments.name: Jason
comments.body:
As Kristof points out, the playing field has indeed shifted in the power dynamics between China and the U.S. How much this turn is part of inevitable and irreversible American decline—a trendy narrative—remains to be seen. I would agree with Mr. Kristof’s view that such brazen declarations of the “end of the American age” may be both overwrought and premature.
In the midst of rapidly shifting geopolitical ground, the edge the U.S. has in A.I. development should neither be understated nor underplayed. We should be careful not to squander this advantage through some of the more restrictive regulatory approaches currently being advocated. A.I. remains one of the few remaining important areas where the U.S. still “holds the cards.”
Trump and Xi could indeed initiate talks that lead to sensible progress on A.I. safety. Considering what’s at stake in ensuring the U.S. does not lose its advantage on the A.I. frontier, any government regulation of the U.S.’s domestic A.I. models has to start and stop with verifiable international agreements.

The eradication of China expertise from the diplomatic and intelligence agencies, coupled with a Trumpian war on think tanks, underscores our intellectual weakness in dealing with Xi and China. comments.name: Philly-Girl
comments.body:
Whether you think it’s cheating or not, the LW has negative feelings about the practice of anonymous sexting. I would too. It seems like the BF is addicted to the behavior.

The LW seems thoughtful and caring.  
But I do sense that she may try to sublimate her true feelings by bargaining with herself around his behavior, that most likely will not change. 

Too often young women stay in relationships that are not right for them, in the hope that things will change, get better or they try to acquiesce to the behavior they find troubling, resulting in more turmoil and upset.

Listen to your inner voice, and take care of yourself.  End this relationship with discretion.  Don’t waste your precious time in college, your youth, bogged down by a relationship that ultimately is not right for you.

I encourage anyone reading this to try and organize locally; whether your neighbors are Republican or Democrat, conservative or liberal, anyone who is on the side of AI regulation and humanity is welcome. During the month left before the midterms, put pressure on politicians of all stripes to take a stance on AI and slow the current pace of AI development nationally, and then push for diplomacy with China.

These are frightful times. But this is also an incredible opportunity, -- the arrival of a technology so imminent and dangerous that it clarifies the values all humans share.

This is a fight that demands humanity be at its best and kindest, and could finally bring us together. So let's fight for humanity.

We ran that experiment and what we see is that when the people who know these systems in the deepest possible ways (Hinton, Bengio, Russell, etc) are raising every conceivable warning imaginable, half the world reacts with conspiratorial fervor, dismissing it all as a psyop, a hoax, or cynical self-interest.  The margin for error on ASI is really narrow, if it even exists at all.  Imagining that, if a kill switch were in place we would somehow coordinate to use it, when we cannot coordinate on the need to even have one, is delusion.  Bleak times.

comments.name: Lake Monster

Nature offers few reassuring examples: when organisms with vastly different capabilities compete, the weaker rarely controls the stronger simply through good intentions. AI safety therefore depends on solving alignment before capability outruns our ability to reliably understand, constrain, and correct the systems we create.

comments.body: As a student at Columbia, I researched these exact glaciers. What's terrifying is that these glaciers in the Hindu-Kush Himalaya are some of the fastest receding in the world, and as they continue to lose structural integrity glacial lake outburst floods and slope failures like this will only continue to happen. These glaciers also feed Asia's largest rivers - the Amu Darya, Ganges, Indus, Irrawaddy, Mekong, Salween, Tarim, Yangtze, Brahmaputra, and Yellow River - which in turn are crucial to agriculture throughout Asia. As we lose these glaciers, what will happen to the food supply they support? Praying for the victims.

comments.name: Ramkihosur
comments.body: The Space Applications Centre of ISRO estimates that the Himalayas contain more than 30,000 glaciers, holding about 600 billion tons of ice. These glaciers feed rivers that sustain hundreds of millions of people across nations from Afghanistan to Myanmar, and even further downstream in the Mekong basin, supporting countries like Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, and Thailand.he Himalayas are geologically fragile, prone to erosion and landslides. Accelerated melting increases the likelihood of avalanches and destabilises ecosystems. The fate of Asia’s rivers—and the wellbeing of billions including India —depends on how urgently we respond to the Himalayan meltdown.

comments.name: Amelia
comments.body: It can feel easy to reciprocate a feeling of envy in a “perfect” seeming world where everyone’s successes are constantly displayed. As a teenager it is difficult not to compare yourself when you feel like everyone has their life together in some way through academics, sports, or physical appearances. However, when changing your perspective envy can be seen as “an alarm bell that shows you what’s important to you” (Passarella). In addition, social scientist Stacy S. Kim asserts that it is necessary to normalize feeling envious because “when we compare, we inevitably look up to those doing better or having more” striving us an individual to do more (Kim). The article as a whole took a different approach on the false narrative surrounding “envy” as a negative, shameful term. As the reader I feel encouraged to not let comparison define me, but as a boost that allows me to succeed to new heights.

comments.name: Mara
comments.body: I personally do not believe that envy is a natural feeling. I think it is natural to want things other people have; I personally find myself wanting to be as pretty or as talented as someone else someone around me or even online. But this in itself is not envy. Envy is a feeling of discontented or resentful longing aroused by someone else's possessions, qualities, or luck. It is natural to want something, but it is not natural to resent a person for having that thing.

comments.name: Abigail Valenzuela
comments.body: There haven't been many times where I wished to be someone else or have something someone else has. Though, there was this one point in my life where I was so unbearably envious of a girl I never knew. She was tall, bright, smart, charismatic, had the most beautiful smile any person could ever lay eyes on. But none of those things compared to the real reason why I was so envious of her. There was this boy, of course, that I was so madly in love with for years, and they ended up together. My initial response was to be happy for them, but the boy was one of my closest friends, and he would tell me everything that would go on in their relationship. I tried for so long to keep myself calm and composed, but every word he spoke to me about her was like a straight piercing, burning arrow through my soul. After a few months, their relationship became something so overwhelmingly toxic and manipulative, they ended up breaking up. I felt so terrible, because it felt so good to hear that they separated. I only then realized how dangerous envy and jealousy could be, especially to a young girl's teenage heart. As I matured and moved on, I continued to keep that envy in my memory, only to internalize the effects and grow from those distasteful feelings. Dr. Kim states, “Envy is not just wanting, it’s an alarm bell that shows you what’s important to you". This quote doesn't convey any bad relations to envy. Instead, it declares how envy can be used to see the true passions of your heart.

comments.name: Kayla Soto
comments.body: Envy is a feeling that I have experienced a lot more than I would like to admit. But hearing that it is normal for everyone to feel envy at times gives me a little more peace of mind. I find myself being more envious of my peers and of their accomplishment. For instance, I find I get really envious of my peers when they get a higher score than me and they make a comment like, “I didn’t even study for the test.” I get envious because, how did you get a higher score than me, when I put the effort into studying the material, and you didn’t make the effort at all. A part of the article that stood out to me the most was when Stacy S. Kim described envy as an “alarm bell that shows you what’s important to you.” This makes me feel a lot better about all the times I have gotten jealous of a peer getting a higher score than me on an assignment or test; because all along it was just a sign of how much I value my education. A piece of advice I could give to another young person experiencing or receiving envy is don’t allow it to make you feel guilty or bad about it. It is a normal experience in life and at some point everyone feels envious, but don’t let it stop you from continuing to excel in whatever it may be that is making that other person envious of you.

comments.name: Melody
comments.body: To me, envy is a natural part of life. When there are always many accomplished people around you, you can’t help but feel jealous of their possessions or achievements. Passarella notes that being around people “makes envy impossible to avoid” (Passarella, as cited in Doyne). Honestly, I do feel envious more often than I would like to admit. Whenever I catch myself stewing in these thoughts, I feel shameful; I believe I shouldn’t think of my friends and peers that way. Hearing that it is normal certainly helps me view envy in a better light. I know that it can’t be controlled, but hearing that other people experience it often too helps me see envy as a naturally occurring phenomenon instead of something horrible. After reading this article and thinking about envy further, I argue that feeling envious is not an issue; it’s what you choose to do with that feeling that matters. Instead of constantly thinking about what you don’t have or can’t do, you can take action and make yourself better so you can reach new heights. Using envy to better yourself is much more productive than viewing it negatively. For example, I become envious whenever I hear of someone who has accomplished more than me. Rather than pushing them down and belittling their achievements, I try to work harder so I can get to the same level of success as they are. Therefore, using envy as a tool for improvement rather than an excuse to downplay someone else is essential to leading a better life.

comments.name: Evelyn Carle

Whether it's my friends or people I don't know online, hearing about or seeing people go out and do things like a city trip, a sports game, a vacation, or any outing with friends, or even alone, I find myself envious that I'm not experiencing things like that in my own life. It's like a more aggressive “FOMO.” I think envy is a really human thing, but I know it comes from an illogical place; I do build fun memories and experiences like that all the time, and envy ignores that. I openly advocate for me and my friends to be kinder, to channel any envious feelings into being happy for what other people get to do, and to be supportive of our friends instead of bringing them down.

For example, it can be hard not to feel jealous when someone gets an opportunity that I wanted or is recognized for is something I have been working on. Ms. Passarella writes that it is “natural” to envy your friends, and hearing that makes the feeling seem less embarrassing. I think many people pretend they never feel jealous because they do not want to sound mean or ungrateful. However, recognizing envy can help us understand what we value or what goals we want to reach. Instead of letting jealousy turn into resentment, I try to turn it into motivation by practicing, working toward my own goals and congratulations friends. Knowing envy is normal, it does not mean we should let it control our actions, but it can remind us to focus on improving ourselves.

comments.body: Oregon seems to follow the general common law rule that a landowner has a right of lateral support. As an aside, NY does also, and has statutory provisions. In this case, if work is done on a nearby property, such as deep excavation, that property owner would be liable for damages resulting on a neighbor's property caused by the loss of lateral support. Precautions can and should be taken when deep excavation occurs, such as the construction of retaining walls. Of course, the party asserting the claim would need to demonstrate that the excavation caused the loss of lateral support which caused the damage. The issuance of a permit or CO for the work does not absolve the owner having the work performed of liability, and it does not, as a general principle, result in liability on the part of the municipal agency issuing the permit or CO. As to the damaged landowner's property insurance policy covering it, that is more murky an issue. A careful reading of the policy is needed, but my guess is it would not be covered. If a piece of excavation equipment crashed into the LW's house, yes that would be covered, but likely not in this scenario.

I live in the American West and we are experiencing a prolonged drought. The heat was oppressive this summer. And when we did get rain, it was in downpours. The soil in my yard is changing from loam to sand. My home's foundation is shifting. My basement is sinking. 

I am very angry at the politicians who have done little to nothing to address the climate crisis. 

I hold on to the words of Jonas Salk who said "our greatest responsibility is to be good ancestors." 

I'm doing my best ever since I saw An Inconvenient Truth twenty years ago. We must vote all the climate change deniers out of office and push our government officials to treat this issue with the seriousness and urgency it deserves. 

I'm canvassing among my neighbors, getting out the vote for November. I've insulated my small house, put on solar panels, gotten an entry level EV and charger in my garage and a heat pump to heat and cool my small home. 

I encourage all those who are able to go electric to do so. And get involved in local politics. And vote. And consume less. We must all consume far less. And think upon other species are our kin.

What has given me the most joy is planting native shrubs, flowers, grasses and trees in my small yard for the pollinators and birds. The loss of biodiversity is a twin crisis to climate change. It gives me hope to see my neighbors do the same. We also put out water for the birds and turn off our outdoor lights during bird migration which is happening now. Please join us.

comments.name: James Jordan

I’ve worked in energy and environmental policy since the 1970s, when I served as Director of the Navy’s Energy R&D program. Even then, our researchers understood that burning coal, oil, and natural gas was altering atmospheric physics and warming the planet’s air and oceans.

In 1979, I joined the staff of the Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee and Defense Appropriations Committee, beginning a long public‑policy effort to help the country move toward a post‑carbon economy. The consensus among researchers was clear: invest in innovations that could succeed in global markets, build the foundation of a sustainable Electric Century, and rigorously monitor greenhouse‑gas emissions. We all knew the transition would be slow, because modern prosperity had been built on carbon‑intensive technologies from automobiles to coal‑fired power to steel and cement.

In 1992, I joined Al Gore, John Kerry, and others at the Rio Earth Summit. It was a moment of genuine optimism, with promising technologies and serious international engagement. For a time, it felt like real momentum.

But around 2000, the issue became deeply politicized in the U.S., and we lost much of the enthusiasm that Rio generated. Still, the sustained work of leaders like Al Gore, John Kerry, and Joe Biden has kept the vision of a market‑driven Electric Century alive.

We are in a slowdown, now, but I am confident the global market will continue to adapt its standard of living to sustainable energy.

There was no physical evidence linking him to the crime, and the DNA recovered from the victim didn't match him, yet they won a conviction built on a confession he quickly retracted. Jeffrey, still a teenager, must have felt like he had no one on his side. Years later, when he sought DNA testing, Jeanine Pirro's office refused. He was exonerated in 2006 after 16 years in prison, when DNA identified the real killer. Why didn't anyone protect Jeffrey? He should never have spent a day in a cell.

comments.name: Sisyphus
comments.body: Wrongful convictions unquestionably occur, and when compelling evidence establishes innocence, those responsible deserve freedom, compensation and our sympathy. But the word “exonerated” is now often used as though it always means factual innocence. It does not. Some convictions are overturned because of procedural errors, unavailable witnesses or changes in prosecutorial policy, even though a jury originally heard the evidence and unanimously found guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. That distinction deserves far more scrutiny than it receives here. Our current criminal-justice culture too often centers defendants while victims and their families disappear from the story. The same city leadership that attends celebrations with people accused or convicted of serious crimes frequently treats law abiding landlords as moral villains. Compassion is admirable, but it should not replace evidence, accountability or concern for victims.

comments.name: Troy Closson
comments.body: Over the past few months, our photographer, Peter, and I talked to New Yorker after New Yorker who felt like this summer was special in some way. So many were trying to be outside more than usual. And it was almost surprising to hear how they still brought up the pandemic, the isolation it brought on — and how much the communal spirit in the city stood in opposition to it.

articles.title: The Summer New York City Stayed Outside
articles.summary: For many people in the city, the past few months fostered desperately needed moments of communal bliss — and evoked a surprising feeling.
